title: Asian-Style Sesame Coleslaw
subtitle: Crunchy cabbage and carrot slaw with sesame-ginger dressing
excerpt: A crunchy, vibrantly dressed slaw of white and red cabbage, carrot and spring onion, tossed in a sesame-ginger-rice vinegar dressing with a little soy. Lighter than mayo-based versions and very good alongside grilled fish or tofu.
sourceNotes: Asian-style slaws with sesame-ginger dressings became common in Anglo-American home cooking from the late 1990s, driven by the popularity of fusion cuisine. The dressing draws on Japanese and Chinese condiment traditions (sesame oil, rice vinegar, soy sauce) adapted for a Western slaw format.

recipe.batchNotes: Keeps well for up to 2 days in the fridge. The cabbage softens as it sits.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Rest for at least 20 minutes before serving so the cabbage softens slightly.

content.text: Asian-style slaw dresses shredded cabbage with rice vinegar, toasted sesame oil, soy and fresh ginger instead of mayonnaise. It stays crunchy longer than a mayo slaw, has a clean sharpness, and works particularly well alongside anything grilled, teriyaki-style, or fried in breadcrumbs.

items.prepNote: coarsely grated or cut into thin matchsticks

content.text: Whisk together {{rice-vinegar}} of rice vinegar, {{sesame-oil}} of toasted sesame oil, {{soy-sauce-light}} of light soy sauce, the grated ginger, {{rapeseed-oil}} of rapeseed oil and {{honey}} of honey. Taste: the dressing should be lightly sweet, sharp and savoury.

Toss the white and red cabbage, carrot and spring onion together in a large bowl. Pour the dressing over and toss until everything is coated. Leave to rest for 20 minutes before serving. Scatter the sesame seeds and coriander (if using) over the top just before serving.

items.cause: Sesame oil can vary in strength between brands.
items.fix: Add another half teaspoon of sesame oil and a little more soy to deepen the flavour. Taste and adjust.

items.cause: Red cabbage can be bitter, especially raw.
items.fix: Add an extra teaspoon of honey and toss well. Resting for longer softens the bitterness.

content.text: This slaw fits alongside a wide range of dishes that a mayo-based coleslaw would overpower. Salmon teriyaki, crispy tofu, chicken thighs roasted with soy and ginger, beef skewers with peanut sauce: all of these benefit from a fresh, sharp counterpoint rather than a rich creamy one. The sesame-ginger dressing is one of the more useful things to know how to make.
